thread: Follow a building from its raw parts through the hands and tools that shape it, then step inside the finished structures. The swarm can become a brick, a carpenter's plane, a timber joint, or a roof sheltering a whole room.

candidates.name: Miles Lewis Heritage Building Materials Collection
candidates.why: A university collection of bricks, lime and cement, finishes, ironmongery and roofing gives the swarm a cabinet of building parts and material textures to inhabit.

candidates.name: Weald & Downland Living Museum
candidates.why: Carpenters' planes, augers and chisels meet pegged timber joints, historic building fragments and a modern timber gridshell: a workshop full of tools and structures coming together.

candidates.name: Ballenberg Swiss Open-Air Museum
candidates.why: Swiss houses and outbuildings offer thatch, stone-weighted shingles, timber framing, tiled stoves, granaries and drying kilns for the swarm to assemble into places.

candidates.name: Chiltern Open Air Museum
candidates.why: Rescued buildings range from a thatched barn and timber-framed cottage to a tin chapel, forge and prefabricated house, each with its own shape and history.

candidates.name: The Wood Database
candidates.why: Hundreds of wood species and guides to grain, pores, strength and drying let the swarm begin as a richly patterned building material.

candidates.name: Science Museum Group Collection
candidates.why: Its hand and machine tool collections include moulding planes, brace drills and saws, while engineering models show how shaped parts become larger structures.

candidates.name: National Building Museum
candidates.why: Architectural models, building fragments, material samples and construction drawings invite the swarm to explore buildings at several scales.

candidates.name: HistoricBridges.org
candidates.why: Photographed bridges and guides to trusses, arches and other structural forms offer an ending where beams and joints grow into crossings.
